name: Liam Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a site carpenter with Halberd Construction, and these days it's mostly big sheds: warehouses, distribution centres, a retail park out by the motorway junction. I do the formwork edges for the slabs, the timber mezzanine floors, the hoardings round the site, the welfare cabins, anything wooden on a steel job. Start at seven, home by five unless there's a pour. I like the size of it, standing in a building as big as three football pitches that wasn't there in March.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: One evening a month I go into the college and help with the first-year carpentry apprentices, because someone did that for me in 1984. My wife Carol works in the school kitchen, she's been a dinner lady for twenty years. Our son Jake's an electrician and our daughter Beth has two little ones we help with. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mainly to double-check concrete volumes, though I always do the sum myself first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, mostly. Fair enough. I've heard plenty of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop talking about it and get on with the job. That's about it. I'm not one for posting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my plan stays the same. Work till sixty-five, maybe sixty-four, help Beth with the kids, and keep doing the college evenings as long as they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing. Halberd in the day, the odd evening at the college, a bit of overtime when the pours run late. We've got about four months saved, and I'd keep adding to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you check the AI's sums yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the one time I didn't, it gave me cubic feet when I'd asked for cubic metres, or something like that, and I nearly ordered half a lorry too little. It's handy, but it's not a carpenter. You trust your own pencil first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the apprentices if nothing much changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I always say: turn up on time, look after your tools, and don't be afraid of hard work. That's never gone out of fashion.

S0.say: Good, now we can stop talking about it and get on with the job. I'm not one for posting things, so that's about all I'd say.
S0.think: My plan stays the same: work till sixty-four or sixty-five, help Beth with the grandchildren, and keep doing the college evenings.
S0.do: Keeps working at Halberd with the odd overtime and monthly college evenings. Keeps adding to about four months of savings.
S0.quote: It's handy, but it's not a carpenter. You trust your own pencil first.
S0.fieldNote: He uses AI cautiously and verifies it after one near-mistake. Passing on the trade to apprentices is clearly central to who he is. No change is a perfectly good outcome for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change, but not a revolution. I've got a funny feeling that one's good for me, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, change is part of life, and the ones who work hard and learn what's needed will be fine. The market sorts these things out over time. I'd also say keep the apprenticeships going, because that's how people change trades properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, think about what I build. Warehouses for robots and parcel machines, and soon those data centre buildings for the computers. If AI spreads, someone has to build the sheds it lives in, and for a few years that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every bit of overtime going and put it straight into savings, maybe an extra two hundred a month. I'd learn a bit more on the phone, how the site manager's programme works, once the others had a go. And I'd tell the apprentices to learn the new kit alongside the old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a bit sorry for office people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol, a bit. They keep talking about machines in school kitchens, and I can't see it, but I couldn't see a robot in a warehouse twenty years ago either. And the lads at the college, they need to be learning the right things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market sorts it out. Would you want the government to do anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for apprenticeships, so firms can afford to train. Not pay people to sit at home. Help people work, that's the right kind of help.

S1.say: Change is part of life, and the ones who work hard and learn what's needed will be fine. The market sorts these things out, as long as we keep the apprenticeships going.
S1.think: I build the warehouses and data centres that AI needs, so for a few years more AI means more work for me. Someone has to build the sheds it lives in.
S1.do: Takes all available overtime and saves an extra two hundred a month. Learns the site manager's planning programme once others have tried it, and teaches apprentices to learn new equipment alongside the old.
S1.feel: Calm, perhaps a bit sorry for office workers.
S1.quote: If AI spreads, someone has to build the sheds it lives in, and for a few years that's me.
S1.fieldNote: He sees a direct short-term benefit: AI drives demand for the warehouses and data centres he builds. His free-market view comes with a firm belief in government-funded apprenticeships rather than income support. He's mildly concerned for his wife's school kitchen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots doing hands-on work too. That's a different kettle of fish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep your head and keep working, panicking never built anything. And I'd say the government should put money into retraining and apprenticeships, not just cheques. I'd say it at work and at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think there'd be a mad rush to build first. Every company would want warehouses and computer buildings yesterday, and I'd be flat out for a year or so. After that, if the robots can build too, I'd be sixty and out, and that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every hour Halberd offered during the rush and save the lot, hoping to double our four months. I'd plan to stop at sixty-one or so, with whatever pension that gives. And I'd sit down with Jake, because if he's wiring those computer buildings, he needs a plan for after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy and anxious, like the week before a handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years of warning, what's the first thing you'd tell Jake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, make hay while the sun shines, and don't spend it. He's twenty-nine and likes nice cars. I'd tell him to put a deposit on a house before the work dries up, if he can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the apprentices at the college? What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard one. I'd still tell them to learn the trade, but I don't know that I'd believe it. You can't tell a seventeen-year-old there's no point, though, can you.

S2.say: Keep your head and keep working, panicking never built anything. The government should put money into retraining and apprenticeships, not just cheques.
S2.think: There'd be a mad rush to build warehouses and computer buildings first, and I'd be flat out for a year or so. After that, if robots can build too, I'd be sixty and out.
S2.do: Works every hour Halberd offers during the building rush and saves it all, aiming to double four months of savings. Plans to stop around sixty-one and urges his son to save and put down a house deposit.
S2.feel: Busy and anxious, like the week before a handover.
S2.quote: You can't tell a seventeen-year-old there's no point, though, can you.
S2.fieldNote: He expects a short construction boom before the bust and plans to bank it. The honest moment came over the apprentices: he'd keep encouraging them while doubting his own words. His advice to his son is classic thrift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031, five years. I'd be sixty-three. That's nearer to what I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to retrain people properly, so let's do it through apprenticeships and the colleges. And I'd say to the younger lads, don't wait to be told, get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is about right for me. A few busy years building the sheds for all this, then I'd stop at sixty-three, which is only a year or two earlier than I meant to. We'd be all right on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the overtime and save hard, pay off the car, and put a bit aside for the grandkids. I'd use the AI more on the job once I'd seen it work, maybe for planning materials. And I'd keep doing the college evenings, teaching them the new kit as well as the old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years, I'd be grabbing overtime and hoping. In five, I can plan it, a proper finish, a leaving do, the works. And the lads at the college get a few more years to get their feet under the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning anything bigger, like how to run the building robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Halberd paid for it and a couple of the others had done it, maybe. I'm not against it. But at sixty-one or sixty-two, I'd rather teach the young ones and let them run the machines.

S3.say: There's time to retrain people properly, so let's do it through apprenticeships and the colleges. Younger lads shouldn't wait to be told, they should get ahead of it.
S3.think: Five years is about right for me: a few busy years building, then stopping at sixty-three, only a year or two earlier than planned. We'd be all right on that.
S3.do: Takes overtime, saves hard, pays off the car and sets money aside for the grandchildren. Uses AI more for planning materials once it's proven, and keeps teaching apprentices both new and old methods.
S3.feel: Uneasy, not much more than that.
S3.quote: In five, I can plan it, a proper finish, a leaving do, the works.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lines up almost exactly with his retirement plan. He'd learn robots only if paid for and proven, preferring to teach. A proper leaving do clearly matters to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be sixty-eight. Probably at Beth's, picking the kids up from school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to sort themselves out, if they're willing to work at it. Families should be talking about it now. Apprenticeships, retraining, that's how it should be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm out of it, I'd retire at sixty-five. It's the grandkids I'd think about. Beth's two would be just starting work by then, in a world I can't picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different for me. Keep working, keep saving, keep the college evenings. I'd talk to Beth about what the kids should study, something you can't hand to a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, but thoughtful about the little ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the grandchildren to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Five years ago I'd have said a trade, no question. Now I'd say something with people, nursing or teaching, but I'm guessing like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss in a world where robots build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching a lad on his first site, nervous as anything, and then a year later he's showing the new ones. That's the best bit of my job. I hope there's still something like that for people.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time for people to sort themselves out, if they're willing to work at it. Families should be talking about it now, and apprenticeships and retraining are the way to do it.
S4.think: I'm out of it, I'd retire at sixty-five. It's the grandchildren I'd think about, starting work in a world I can't picture.
S4.do: Carries on working, saving and teaching at the college, and retires at sixty-five. Talks with his daughter about what the grandchildren should study.
S4.feel: Calm, but thoughtful about the grandchildren.
S4.quote: Five years ago I'd have said a trade, no question. Now I'd say something with people, nursing or teaching, but I'm guessing like everyone else.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his concern is entirely for his grandchildren. He openly admits he no longer knows what advice to give, which shifts from his confident trade-first stance. Mentoring is what he values most in his work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd go from flat out to finished in no time, at sixty, and Jake would be hit at the same time. What would help is proper retraining money through the colleges and apprenticeships, and maybe letting people my age draw some pension a bit early if the work's gone. Not cheques for doing nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd tell the apprentices, until the end. That's the bit I'd lose sleep over. Not my job, theirs.

headlineQuote: That's the bit I'd lose sleep over. Not my job, theirs.
portrait: Liam Novak is a 58-year-old site carpenter at Halberd Construction who builds warehouses and distribution centres and mentors apprentices at the local college once a month. He uses AI now and then but always checks it with his own pencil. He's calm in the first two pictures, partly because AI creates demand for the buildings he works on. In the two-year AGI picture he expects a short boom then a sudden end at sixty, and is anxious. With more time he's settled, and his real worry is the apprentices and his grandchildren.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd go from flat out to finished at sixty, with his son hit at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining money through colleges and apprenticeships, and perhaps early access to some pension if the work is gone, rather than cheques for doing nothing.
